summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, and its own Sharia legislature has moved to re-criminalise conduct struck down at federal level. On 13 August 2026 the Kelantan state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026, which replaces the 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down in February 2024 on federalism grounds. The new enactment legislates decency and aurat-covering offences and, in terms, regulates gender change under Islamic criminal law; enforcement has run from 2026.

Clause 15 of the bill obliges Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law, and the bill carries an explicit provision on gender change. These offences reach Muslims only; a non-Muslim visitor in Kelantan falls under the federal Penal Code alone, while a Muslim visitor or resident is exposed to the state Sharia regime as applied by the Kelantan Syariah enforcement authorities.

The Kelantan Syariah courts have already begun applying the gender-change provision. A February 2026 case, which preceded the bill, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court matter involving gender change, and the new decency and gender-change provisions are in force and being applied by those courts. Because the enactments contain no statutory definition of transgender presentation, the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by enforcement officers on the ground.
tangentialFactors:
The Federal Court's February 2024 ruling against 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions rested on which legislature may enact the offence, not on whether cross-dressing or gender nonconformity may be punished. Kelantan's 2026 bill is a direct legislative response to that federalism holding, restoring the substance of the struck-down provisions under a restructured instrument rather than conceding the underlying prohibition.

The pattern of state-level re-legislation after the Selangor cross-dressing provision was struck down in February 2021 and Kelantan's provisions in February 2024 indicates that adverse Sharia judgments in Malaysia have produced replacement enactments, not decriminalisation. Nothing under the federal Penal Code has been decriminalised either.
localsOnly:
For Muslim residents of Kelantan, the practical effect of the 2026 enactment is that gender change, dress presentation and matters of modesty are now expressly regulated under state Islamic criminal law, with Kelantan's Syariah courts actively adjudicating gender-change cases as of February 2026. Penalties under Kelantan's Sharia regime reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and Sharia courts may additionally order counselling or institutional rehabilitation for up to six months.

The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery, though never gazetted and not legally binding, is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes; the 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court order requiring the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card was overturned on appeal in 2017, and no successful marker change has been documented since the historical 1975 recognition of Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the specific penalties attached to Clause 15 or the gender-change provision of the 2026 Kelantan bill; the RM5,000 fine, three-year term and six strokes of caning cited here are the documented ceilings for Kelantan's pre-existing Sharia offences and may not carry over unchanged to the new instrument. Whether the 2026 enactment has been gazetted and the precise commencement date beyond "enforcement beginning 2026" are not sourced.

No Kelantan-specific incident data on arrests, strip-searches or violence against transgender people appears in this inventory; the documented pattern of arbitrary arrest and detention abuse is national in scope and belongs to the parent record. There is likewise no Kelantan-specific information on airport screening, document checks at entry, or visa treatment of transgender visitors.
